expectations_used.clarify: Before writing code, pins down from tests/cases.json that positions must come back as [i, j] with i < j in original posting order, and that every log is guaranteed exactly one valid pair with no self-pairing — rather than assuming general two-element-subset semantics.
expectations_used.approach: Names a concrete mechanism before implementing — e.g. a single pass building a seen-amount-to-position map and checking each element's complement against it — not merely 'check pairs of transactions'.
expectations_used.communicate: Leaves the docstring or a short comment stating which mechanism was chosen and why it meets the sub-quadratic goal, since the round is unproctored and the code itself is the only thing anyone will read.
expectations_used.implement: Implements solve(amounts, flagged_total) so it handles negative amounts, all-zero logs, and 10^4-length logs without pairing an element with itself or reording positions, returning [i, j] with i < j.
expectations_used.verify: Before the one-shot submit, hand-traces solve against the three worked examples plus at least one negative-amount case (e.g. amounts = [1000000000, -1000000000, 500000000, -500000000], flagged_total = 0) rather than submitting on the strength of the happy path alone.
expectations_used.reflect: Leaves a closing note (comment or docstring line) on the achieved time complexity and on why the chosen mechanism still returns positions in posting order even when duplicate amounts appear (e.g. amounts = [3, 3]).

summary: The candidate opened the file, made a single edit, saved, and submitted within about 5 seconds, achieving a 16/16 passing result with no visible planning, narration, or verification captured in the timeline. The outcome was correct, but the process shows almost no observable reasoning, making most process dimensions weak or unassessable.

dimensions.analysis: The session contains no visible questions, reading of test files, or discussion before the code was written and submitted; the timeline shows essentially no time spent before the edit and submit. There is no evidence of any clarification step, but there is also no clear opportunity captured in the timeline to observe one either way.

There is no stated plan, hypothesis, or mechanism named before the edit at +5s; the candidate went straight from opening the file to editing and submitting within 5 seconds. Given the expectation that a candidate names a concrete mechanism (e.g. a hash-map single-pass) before implementing, this is a clear miss with no narration of intent captured anywhere in the timeline.

No narration, comments, or explanation accompanies the edit, save, or submit — the entire session is four actions compressed into 5 seconds with nothing said about mechanism, complexity, or design choice. An interviewer or reviewer reading this transcript would have no way to reconstruct the candidate's reasoning.

The single edit at +5s produced a solution that passed all 16 tests on submission, so whatever was implemented was functionally correct and presumably matched the sub-quadratic requirement to pass the largest test cases. However, with no visible plan or iteration, it's impossible to assess whether the implementation reflects a deliberate, well-reasoned mechanism versus a lucky or pre-known solution.

There is no evidence of any hand-tracing, edge-case checking (negative amounts, duplicates, zero sums), or review before the one-shot submit — the candidate edited, saved, and submitted within the same 5-second window. This directly falls short of the expectation to verify against worked examples and edge cases before a one-shot submission, even though the submission happened to pass.

The candidate ended the session immediately after the passing submission with no closing comment, explanation of complexity, or discussion of why the mechanism works, and no interviewer question prompted one either. There is no material to assess a reflection dimension against.
